They can produce a similar-looking commit, but they do different things to history and carry different consequences.

**The core difference:** `merge --squash` *adds* a commit; `rebase -i` with squash *replaces* commits.

`git merge --squash other` computes the merge result (diff between `other` and the merge base, merged with your branch) and stages it — then stops. It writes nothing until you `git commit`. The commit you make has **one parent**: your branch tip. Git records no merge, so it does not know `other` was ever integrated.

`git rebase -i main` with `squash`/`fixup` takes your existing commits, replays them, and folds them into one — the original commits are discarded and new ones with new hashes take their place on the same branch.

| | `merge --squash` | rebase -i squash |
|---|---|---|
| Operates on | two divergent branches | one branch's own commits |
| Result | new commit, **1 parent** | new commit, rewritten ancestry |
| Leaves you | changes staged, you commit | commit created by the rebase |
| Rewrites hashes | no | yes |
| Needs force-push if pushed | no | yes |
| Other branch seen as merged | **no** | n/a (same branch) |
| Conflict resolution | once, via merge machinery | per-commit, or at the squash step |
| Authorship/message | you write it fresh | first commit's author; you edit combined message |

**Why the "seen as merged" row matters most.** After `merge --squash`, `git branch --merged` won't list the source branch, and git has no merge base recorded. A later real `git merge other` will try to merge *all* of `other` again — the squashed content is already there, so you get conflicts or duplicated changes. That's why the workflow pairs `--squash` with deleting the source branch. A real merge (`git merge --no-ff`, or GitHub's "Squash and merge" which deletes the branch for you) records the parentage and avoids this.

**When each is the right tool:**

- Squashing *someone else's* branch / a PR into your line, where you can't or shouldn't rewrite their commits → `merge --squash`.
- Cleaning up *your own* local commits before sharing them → rebase. Rewriting is safe exactly when nobody else has the old hashes; a force-push to a shared branch is the failure case to avoid.

**Minor practical notes:** `--squash` uses the merge strategy (rename detection, merge drivers), so it can handle divergence better than patch replay. In rebase, `fixup` silently drops the later commit messages, `squash` opens an editor to combine them; the resulting commit keeps the *first* commit's author and timestamp.
